card_quote: Reading: popular science and psychology (Freakonomics/Gladwell-style); has met the Stanford prison experiment and Milgram in pop books and probably not the critiques. / Constraints: dislikes books without sources; checks Wikipedia when a claim surprises him.
how_read: Cover to cover over two weekends, front matter included, because I always read the copyright page and the 'how this was made' stuff. Played along honestly, ticked sure or guessing, kept score per round. Read the source lines on most entries.

w1_friction.note: There's a placeholder left in the copyright page. Not a great first impression for a book about getting details right.
Appreciate the honesty, but knowing it was AI-drafted made me read every verdict a little more suspiciously.
w1_friction.quote: the entries were drafted with AI tools

w1_friction.note: Back-to-back apple questions. The pairing trick shows up again and again and the second entry usually recycles the first.
w1_friction.quote: Newton himself told of the apple, according to Britannica

w1_friction.note: The stamp says TRUE and the text says it's an embellishment and he never did it. Two lines apart. That's an editing failure, not a nuance.
w1_friction.quote: Franklin never flew a kite in a thunderstorm

w1_friction.note: One Wikipedia article as the whole source list, and the story isn't in the contents or index either.
A 2026 paper saying Dunning-Kruger inverts? That surprised me enough that I'd go look it up before repeating it.
w1_friction.quote: a 2026 reanalysis reports that it inverts

w1_friction.note: A whole disputed verdict on the napkin story resting on a single Wikipedia page. Thin compared to the other entries.
Jargon soup, wrong round header, duplicate number 71, and 'various laboratory studies' as the source. In a book that otherwise cites journals with volume numbers, this stands out badly.
The 'any reason would be invented' line is principled, I guess, but it reads like the writer is reminding itself of a rule.
w1_friction.quote: Any reason offered here would be invented, so none is.

w1_friction.note: Who or what is the 'Law Tome record'? It's referred to everywhere as 'the record' and here it slips into an internal name.
w1_friction.quote: The Law Tome record calls the Hanoi bounty the documented case

w1_friction.note: Ranked by how many people they fooled, based on what data? And several of the page references point to the wrong pages.
w1_friction.quote: The stories that fooled the most people, ranked.

w1_friction.note: Says every entry was read and checked. Then how did the Franklin and goldfish pages get through?
Index sends me to 99 for Benford's law and it's actually two pages later. From round four on, the index and contents drift.

w1_best.why: Stanford prison guards were coached. I'd told that story at dinner as gospel. Genuinely changed my mind, with a real citation.
Milgram's 65 percent being one condition out of twenty-plus. Exactly the nuance my pop-psych books left out.
Levitt and List finding the Hawthorne data and calling it fictional. Great detective story.
Marshmallow test shrinking with a bigger, more diverse sample. Fair and well sourced.
Jevons paradox, with the actual 1865 quote. Smart and current.

w1_flat.why: The goldfish entry in round eight. Unreadable and unsourced.
The Franklin kite entry in round four. Contradicts itself.
Dawkins coined 'meme'. Too easy, and most of the answer is about the selfish gene instead.
Laffer part two, repeats part one.
The answer admits it has no detail on the experiment, so there's nothing there.

w1_review.headline: Smart, well-sourced myth-busting with some sloppy pages
w1_review.body: The psychology round alone is worth it: Stanford prison, Milgram, Hawthorne and the marshmallow test, each with the critiques my pop-science books skipped and real citations to check. The format of guessing first works, and I liked the honesty about disputed cases. But for a book about checking claims, there are too many slips: a leftover placeholder on the copyright page, a Franklin entry whose verdict contradicts its text, a jargon-filled goldfish entry with no real source, and an index that drifts. Bottom line: four stars for content, take a star off for editing.

w2_review_first: Best quick correction to the pop-psychology stories we all repeat that I've seen, and it tells you where each answer came from. A few pages are clearly unfinished, which is ironic for a fact-check book. I'd still recommend it to anyone who reads Gladwell.

w2_lost.why: Thucydides and MAD in round seven, I knew the general idea and the answers felt like summaries of articles.
The goldfish page made me stop and flip back to see if I'd missed an explanation.
Second Laffer entry right after the first, skimmed it.

w2_read_aloud.why: Stanford prison will start a real argument at dinner.
Kitty Genovese, because everyone knows the 38 witnesses and the CCTV study flips it.
Jevons paradox is the smartest thing to bring up when someone talks about efficiency.
Monty Hall and the PhD letters, a guaranteed table debate.
Six degrees being a median of the chains that finished. Neat statistical twist.

w2_book2: Finding the same kind of contradictory or unsourced pages again; once is a slip, twice and I stop trusting the verdicts.
